result.summary: Apollo sends a plague on the Achaeans after Agamemnon insults his priest Chryses. Agamemnon is forced to give up Chryseis, takes Briseis from Achilles, and Achilles withdraws and asks Thetis to have Jove aid the Trojans. Jove grants it, quarrels with Juno, and Vulcan restores peace on Olympus.

scenes.title: Chryses insulted; Apollo's plague
scenes.summary: The poet invokes the Muse. Agamemnon refuses Chryses' ransom, and Apollo answers the priest's prayer with a plague.
scenes.stakes: Chryses risks losing his daughter forever; the Achaeans face death by plague.

scenes.title: The quarrel in assembly
scenes.summary: Achilles calls an assembly, Calchas names the cause, and Agamemnon and Achilles quarrel. Minerva stops Achilles from drawing his sword.
scenes.stakes: Achilles risks his honour and prize; Agamemnon risks his authority; the army faces ruin.

scenes.title: Nestor's plea; Chryseis sent back
scenes.summary: Nestor urges peace in vain and the assembly breaks up. Ulysses takes Chryseis and a hecatomb away, and the army is purified.
scenes.stakes: The unity of the Achaean army.

scenes.title: Briseis taken
scenes.summary: Agamemnon's heralds fetch Briseis from Achilles' tent, and Achilles has Patroclus hand her over.
scenes.stakes: Achilles loses his prize and honour.

scenes.title: Achilles prays to Thetis
scenes.summary: Weeping by the sea, Achilles calls his mother, retells the quarrel and asks her to move Jove to help the Trojans. Thetis promises to go to Olympus.

place.name: the sea shore by the ships

scenes.title: Chryseis returned; Achilles sulks
scenes.summary: Ulysses restores Chryseis to Chryses, they sacrifice to Apollo and feast, and sail back. Achilles stays out of the fighting.

scenes.title: Thetis supplicates Jove
scenes.summary: Thetis clasps Jove's knees and Jove nods to promise honour to Achilles.
scenes.stakes: Jove risks Juno's anger; Achilles' honour depends on his answer.

scenes.title: Jove and Juno quarrel
scenes.summary: Juno suspects Jove and he threatens her. Vulcan soothes her and the gods feast.
scenes.stakes: Juno risks a beating from Jove; the gods' peace at risk.

Patronymic; Menelaus is also a son of Atreus.
Men's name for the monster the gods call Briareus.

notable_quotes.reason: The Iliad's famous opening invocation naming Achilles' anger as its theme.
Achilles' famous insult to Agamemnon: dog-faced wine-bibber.
Achilles laments his short life and denied glory.

analysis.text: The book sets up the poem's theme: Achilles' wrath and wounded honour, caused by a dispute over prizes, which ruin the Achaeans.
Honour in this warrior society is measured by prizes of war, so losing Briseis is a public insult, not only a personal loss.

legacy.text: The opening line became the model for later epic openings invoking the Muse, such as Virgil's Aeneid and Milton's Paradise Lost.
Madeline Miller's novel The Song of Achilles (2011) and the film Troy (2004) draw on the quarrel over Briseis.

fun_facts.text: The Iliad is about 15,000 lines long and covers only a few weeks of the tenth year of the Trojan War.

language_notes.text: Achaeans is one of Homer's names for the Greeks as a whole; Danaans (sentence 15) is another.
The counsels of Jove fulfilled: Jove's plan, which the poem later reveals as honoring Achilles and bringing the Greeks heavy losses.
The son of Jove and Leto is Apollo, identified by his parentage rather than by name.
Suppliant's wreath: a band of wool worn on the sceptre to mark a plea for mercy under divine protection.
Visiting my couch is a euphemism: Agamemnon means she will be his concubine and weave for his household.
Chryse, Cilla, Tenedos and Sminthe are places tied to Apollo's worship; Sminthe may relate to his title Smintheus.
Burned your thigh-bones in fat: a sacrifice in which thigh bones wrapped in fat were burned for the god.
Pyres: stacks of wood on which the dead were cremated.
Achaeans is one of Homer's names for the Greeks; Danaans and Argives, used later, are others.
"Turn roving home" means go wandering back home, drifting by sea rather than with a settled purpose.
A hecatomb is a large public sacrifice, originally of a hundred oxen, offered to a god.
An augur is a seer who reads the will of the gods, here from signs such as birds.
"Swallow his displeasure" means hold back anger for now; "wreaked" means carried out or satisfied his revenge.
"Neither comfort nor performance" means Calchas has never given Agamemnon good news or seen a good prophecy fulfilled.
"Requite you three and fourfold" means repay you three or four times over.
"Shall rue my coming" means whoever's prize Agamemnon takes will regret his arrival.
Phthia is Achilles' homeland in Thessaly, far from Troy, which is why he has no personal grievance against the Trojans.
"Forsooth" is an archaic word meaning "indeed," used here sarcastically.
The Myrmidons are Achilles' own people and soldiers, from Phthia in Thessaly.
"Son of Peleus" and "son of Atreus" are patronymics naming Achilles and Agamemnon by their fathers.
"In two minds" means undecided between two courses of action.
"Rail" means to scold or abuse in harsh words; "vain" means fruitless.
"Hind" is a female deer, a symbol of timidity; "ambuscade" is an ambush.
"You devour your people" means Agamemnon lives off his subjects' goods and labor.
"Facile" here means fluent and effortless: Nestor speaks smoothly and persuasively.
Pirithous, Caeneus, Theseus and the others are heroes of an earlier generation, linked with the Lapith war against the Centaurs, the "mountain savages" of the next sentence.
The goddess mother is Thetis, a sea-goddess; Achilles' divine birth makes him strong but not a king.
"Those that take were those also that gave": the Achaeans gave Chryseis, so they, not Achilles, may take her back. He will not fight over it.
The son of Menoetius is Patroclus, Achilles' close companion.
A hecatomb is a large sacrifice, literally a hundred oxen, offered to a god.
The army purifies itself by washing, to remove the pollution of the plague sent by Apollo.
"Squires" here means attendants or servants; Talthybius and Eurybates are Agamemnon's heralds, who carry messages and act as official envoys.
"Charged them straightly" means he gave strict, firm instructions.
"They shall seek and they shall not find" means the Achaeans will look for Achilles' help in vain.
"To look before and after" means to consider past and future, to think ahead and foresee consequences.
"Loth" is an old spelling of "loath": unwilling, reluctant.
"Hoar" means grey or white, like the foam and mist of the sea.
"Meed" means a reward or prize due for service.
Achilles refers to an earlier tale: Thetis once saved Jove (Saturn's son) when other gods plotted to bind him. The Iliad mentions this only here.
"Rue" means to regret bitterly.
"Twelve days hence" means twelve days from now; the gods' absence delays Thetis' plea.
A hecatomb was a large public sacrifice, literally of a hundred oxen, though the word was used for big offerings generally.
"Propitiate" means to appease a god and win back favour; here, to end the plague Apollo sent.
Refers to Chryses' earlier prayer, when Apollo answered by sending plague on the Greeks as punishment for Agamemnon's refusal to return Chryseis.
A paean is a choral song of praise or thanks, especially to Apollo.
"Gnawed at his own heart" is an idiom for consuming himself with bitter resentment and frustration.
"Son of Saturn" is a patronymic for Jove; Saturn (the Greek Cronos) was his father.
Clasping the knees and touching the chin was the traditional gesture of a suppliant, making a solemn, almost binding appeal for help.
"Requital" means compensation or repayment for a wrong.
"Achaeans" is one of Homer's names for the Greeks.
"Incline your head" means nod; a nod from Jove was a sign of assent.
"Ambrosial" means divine, as if anointed with ambrosia, the food of the gods.
"Upbraid" means to scold or reproach someone severely.
Thetis, a sea goddess, had asked Jove earlier in Book 1 to honor her son Achilles; Juno suspects this.
Clasping someone's knees was the traditional gesture of a suppliant begging a favor.
"Kill much people" is archaic usage: it means kill many men. "Achaeans" is Homer's name for the Greeks.
"Lay my hands about you" means to beat her; Jove threatens physical violence.
"Disquieted" means uneasy or troubled.
Vulcan refers to an earlier occasion when Jove hurled him from heaven for taking Juno's side.
The Sintians were a people of Lemnos, an island in the northern Aegean.
"Hied him" is archaic for hurried or went.

context_notes.text: This is a summary heading for the whole book, not part of the poem's narrative.
Epic poems traditionally open by calling on a Muse, a goddess of inspiration, to supply the story.
Chryses is a priest of Apollo. His daughter Chryseis was taken captive in a raid and given to Agamemnon.
Argos here is Agamemnon's kingdom in Greece, far across the sea from Troy.
Apollo is a god of archery, plague and sudden death, as well as of healing and music.
Juno (the Greek Hera) favours the Greeks and is hostile to Troy. The plague was sent by Apollo.
"Son of Atreus" addresses Agamemnon, the Greek commander-in-chief.
The priest is Chryses, whose daughter Chryseis Agamemnon took as a war prize and refused to ransom.
Clytemnestra is Agamemnon's wife at home. She later murders him after his return.
A prize was a share of war booty, given as a mark of honour. Losing one was a loss of status.
Briseis was Achilles' war prize, a captive woman. Chryseis, Agamemnon's prize, must be returned to her father, Apollo's priest, to end the plague.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) is goddess of wisdom and war. Juno (Hera) favors the Greeks and sends her.
The aegis was a divine shield or breastplate associated with Jove, which Minerva also carries.
Sceptres were symbols of authority held by speakers in assembly; Achilles' oath uses the sceptre as a solemn witness.
Nestor, aged king of Pylos, is the Achaeans' wise elder and frequent peacemaker.
Priam is king of Troy, the Achaeans' enemy.
Ulysses, the Greek Odysseus, is trusted for his cleverness and is sent to return Chryseis safely.
Agamemnon is threatening to take Achilles' prize Briseis in compensation for having to give up his own prize, Chryseis.
Heralds were sacred, inviolable messengers, so Achilles does not blame them.
Thetis is a sea goddess, daughter of the sea-god Nereus, the "old man" of the sea.
Thebe was a city near Troy, sacked by the Greeks earlier in the war; Chryseis was among its captives.
The Ethiopians were a distant people at the edge of the world, favoured by the gods, who often feasted with them.
Chryseis is the daughter of Apollo's priest Chryses; Agamemnon had taken her as a war prize and now returns her.
Chryse, Cilla and Tenedos are places in the northwest of Asia Minor sacred to Apollo, the god of the silver bow, associated with archery, plague and healing.
Wrapping thigh-bones in fat and burning them was the gods' portion; the people then ate the meat themselves.
The gods had been away for twelve days feasting with the Ethiopians, which is why Thetis could not appeal to Jove earlier.
Thetis is a sea goddess. Her son Achilles is fated to die young if he stays at Troy.
Juno (the Greek Hera) is Jove's wife and favours the Greeks, so she would resent his helping the Trojans.
Juno (the Greek Hera) is Jove's wife and sister, and often opposes his plans, especially concerning the Trojan War.
Saturn was Jove's father, a Titan whom Jove overthrew to rule the gods.
Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus) is the lame smith-god, famed as a craftsman.
Nectar was the drink of the gods, as ambrosia was their food.
Apollo is the god of music, and the Muses are goddesses of song and the arts.

literary_notes.text: The poet addresses the goddess and announces the theme, anger, in the first line, setting the epic's focus.
The poet asks who started the quarrel, then answers at once, guiding the audience into the story's cause.
Agamemnon's curt dismissal of the priest's sacred emblems shows his arrogance and disrespect for the gods.
The arrows rattling with the god's rage makes his weapons seem to share his fury.
A face as dark as night conveys Apollo's menace and foreshadows the death he brings.
Calchas's warning that a king nurses revenge anticipates Agamemnon's anger, and the dispute that follows.
Rage "black" and eyes that "flashed fire" turn Agamemnon's anger into vivid images of darkness and flame.
Agamemnon prefers the captive girl to his wife, which shows his possessiveness and pride.
Achilles' insult "steeped in insolence and lust of gain" labels Agamemnon as greedy and arrogant, sharpening the quarrel.
The mountains and "sounding sea" make the distance between Achilles and Troy tangible, and underline his reasons for resentment.
Agamemnon dismisses Achilles' courage by claiming it is merely a gift from the gods.
Minerva's unseen appearance shows the gods directly shaping human choices, and shows Achilles' rage is checked from outside.
Calling Agamemnon dog-faced with a deer's heart insults him as shameless and cowardly.
The sceptre that never regrows becomes an image of the permanent break Achilles swears with the Achaeans.
Achilles predicts the Achaeans' deaths at Hector's hands, anticipating the consequences of his withdrawal.
His words are compared to honey, stressing their sweetness and persuasive charm.
Nestor's three generations of rule establish his age, authority and experience.
Calling Achilles "a tower of strength" presents him as the army's defensive wall.
Achilles' threat of a reddened spear shows his rage rising to violent defiance.
The curling smoke rising to heaven gives a visual picture of the sacrifice reaching the gods.
Achilles complains that Jove has given him a short life without glory. The poem's central tragedy lies in his choice between long life and fame.
Thetis rising "as it were a grey mist out of the waves" gives her a soft, ghostly presence suited to a sea goddess.
Achilles' wish that the Achaeans perish shows how wounded pride makes him vengeful and willing to sacrifice his own comrades.
"Short of life and long of sorrow" balances opposites to sum up Achilles' tragic fate.
"Rosy-fingered Dawn" is a recurring Homeric formula marking the new day.
The foam "hisses" and the ship "flies," giving the sea and vessel lively, almost animate motion.
Achilles' inward-turned anger and longing for battle show his pride and foreshadow the cost of his withdrawal.
Thetis's blunt challenge, daring Jove to refuse openly, shows her desperation and pushes the reluctant god toward a commitment.
Jove's worry about Juno's taunts anticipates the quarrel among the gods that follows later in the book.
The whole mountain shaking at a nod conveys Jove's immense power and the weight of his oath.
Juno's sharp opening insult shows her suspicious, resentful nature and her habit of challenging Jove.
Juno claims she always lets Jove have his way, though her angry accusations just showed the opposite.
Vulcan appears as a peacemaker, treating the gods' quarrel over human affairs as a petty disturbance.
Falling from morning to evening dramatically conveys Jove's immense power and the danger of defying him.
The lame Vulcan bustling as cupbearer makes the gods laugh and turns the tense quarrel into a festive mood.
